title: A late payout lowers your yearly return
body:
Getting your money back later than planned costs you, even if the full amount arrives. Time matters because money returned sooner can be used again. The same total over a longer time means a lower yearly rate.

Example: you lend 1 lakh rupees and expect 1.10 lakh back after 1 year. That is a 10% yearly return. Now suppose the same 1.10 lakh arrives only after 2 years. You still got every rupee, but the yearly return falls to about 4.9%. The delay cut it roughly in half.

This is why a delayed payout is not a small matter, and why tracking the actual dates money came in is useful. A single yearly rate can only be worked out from real dates, not from the totals alone.

What to check: When was each payout due, and when did it actually arrive?

Education, not investment advice.

title: Small yearly fees add up
body:
A fee of 1 or 2 percent a year sounds small. Over many years it takes a large share of what you earn, because the fee is charged again every year on a growing amount, and what is paid in fees stops earning too.

Example: you put in 1 lakh rupees for 10 years. At 8% a year with interest added back, it grows to about 2,15,900 rupees. Now suppose a 2% yearly fee leaves you only 6%. After 10 years you have about 1,79,100 rupees. The fee cost you about 36,800 rupees, even though 2% looked small each year.

The gap grows with time. A fee may be worth paying for a real service, but you should know its size and compare the return after the fee, not before it.

What to check: What are all the yearly charges, and what is the return after them?

Education, not investment advice.

title: Count the payouts you already received
body:
When you look at a holding, its current value is only part of the story. If it paid you money along the way, that money counts as part of what you earned, even though it is no longer inside the holding.

Example: you put in 1 lakh rupees. Over 3 years it paid you 10,000 rupees each year, so 30,000 rupees in total. Now the holding is worth 95,000 rupees. Looking only at the value, it seems you lost 5,000 rupees. But you hold 95,000 and you already received 30,000, so 1,25,000 rupees in total. Your real gain is 25,000 rupees, which is 25%.

Leaving out earlier payouts can make a good holding look bad, and the reverse is also possible. Look at the money you put in, the money you got back, and what is still left.

What to check: Does your view of a holding include every payout you have received so far?

Education, not investment advice.
